clue.text: Some good men inter literary critic

parts.note: holy men, the canonised good, are saints
to inter a body is to bury it

explanation.surface: A note that some virtuous men are laid to rest beside a man of letters.
explanation.walkthrough: George Saintsbury (1845-1933) was a prolific English literary critic and historian of literature.
explanation.definitionFit: George Saintsbury was a celebrated Victorian and Edwardian reviewer and historian of English letters.

clue.text: Farm boy among Flora Poste's ethical problems

indicators.note: the letters sit among the run of words that follows, spanning the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A lad on the farm features in the moral difficulties of the heroine of Cold Comfort Farm.
explanation.walkthrough: Flora Poste is the heroine of Stella Gibbons's Cold Comfort Farm; Seth Starkadder is the brooding young man on the farm, so the hidden name fits the surface too.
explanation.definitionFit: Seth Starkadder is the handsome young son of the family on Cold Comfort Farm.

clue.text: Identity points of critical date

parts.note: ID is the usual short form of identity, as on an ID card
E (east) is a compass point
S (south) is another compass point

explanation.surface: Proof of who you are has several key features on an important day.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ides of March was the day Julius Caesar was warned of and murdered on, hence a fateful date.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Roman calendar the mid-month day, most famously in March when Caesar died, became a byword for a fateful day.

clue.text: Collectors' piece by Scott

parts.note: a collector of old relics is an antiquary, and Walter Scott wrote a novel with that title, so the work is literally a collector's piece

explanation.surface: A prized item for collectors written by Sir Walter Scott.
explanation.walkthrough: Scott's 1816 novel is about Jonathan Oldbuck, an obsessive collector of antiquities; 'Collectors' piece' pretends to mean a valuable item.
explanation.definitionFit: Scott's third Waverley novel takes its title from its hero, an elderly scholar of relics and old coins.

clue.text: Misleading approbation for woman in Leonard title

definitions.text: Misleading approbation for woman in Leonard title

parts.words: Misleading approbation for woman in Leonard title
parts.note: the cry of applause addressed to a female performer appears in an Elmore Leonard title, but there it is a man's surname, so it misleads

explanation.surface: A cheer for a lady that turns up deceptively in a book title by Leonard.
explanation.walkthrough: Elmore Leonard's novel LaBrava is named after its hero Joe LaBrava, a man, so the feminine 'well done!' in the title misleads.
explanation.definitionFit: In Italian applause the feminine form of 'well done' is shouted to a woman, and the word forms half of Leonard's hero's surname.

clue.text: A friar sat puzzled, recognizing emperor

indicators.note: a puzzled mind is muddled, so the letters of these words are jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: A monk sits bewildered when he recognises a monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: Ras Tafari was the name of Haile Selassie, Emperor of Ethiopia, before his coronation.
explanation.definitionFit: Haile Selassie of Ethiopia bore this title and name as regent before being crowned ruler in 1930.

clue.text: Big story of Greek letter in the Community

indicators.note: the Greek letter is placed inside the abbreviation for the Community

parts.note: EC is the European Community
pi is a letter of the Greek alphabet

explanation.surface: A grand narrative about a Greek character living in the European Union.
explanation.definitionFit: A long heroic narrative poem or a sprawling saga is a grand tale on a vast scale.

clue.text: Where one may identify attitudes of Eva Figes

definitions.text: Where one may identify attitudes of Eva Figes

parts.words: Where one may identify attitudes of Eva Figes
parts.note: Eva Figes wrote Patriarchal Attitudes (1970), and the attitudes she attacked are found in male-dominated society

explanation.surface: A question of where to find the views of a feminist writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Eva Figes's feminist study Patriarchal Attitudes examines the male-run social order, which is where those attitudes are to be found.
explanation.definitionFit: A social system ruled by fathers and men generally is the subject of Figes's book.

clue.text: Like dependable support of Greek women

definitions.text: Like dependable support of Greek women

parts.words: Like dependable support of Greek women
parts.note: carved female figures used as columns in Greek temples support the roof, so the support is literally made of Greek women

explanation.surface: Describing the reliable backing given by women of Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: Caryatids are sculpted women serving as pillars, as on the Erechtheion in Athens; 'dependable support' sounds moral but is architectural.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes columns in the form of draped female statues bearing an entablature.

clue.text: In which restoration architect stages deterioration in condition

definitions.text: In which restoration architect stages deterioration in condition

parts.words: In which restoration architect stages deterioration in condition
parts.note: John Vanbrugh, architect and Restoration playwright, staged a comedy whose title means a worsening after recovery

explanation.surface: A builder of restorations puts on show a building's decline.
explanation.walkthrough: Vanbrugh designed Blenheim Palace and wrote the 1696 comedy The Relapse; 'restoration architect' suggests someone who repairs buildings, not a Restoration-era dramatist.
explanation.definitionFit: Vanbrugh's play is titled for a falling back into illness or vice after apparent recovery.

clue.text: Eminent person begotten by H. G. Wells?

definitions.meaning: H. G. Wells wrote a short story of this title about a body hurtling towards Earth

explanation.surface: A great figure fathered by the science-fiction writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Wells's 1897 story The Star describes a celestial body nearly destroying the Earth.
explanation.definitionFit: A celebrity is a luminary, and Wells's story names a celestial body.

clue.text: Mist Napoleon disseminated, disguising thoughts of Plotinus

indicators.note: disseminated means scattered abroad, so the letters of these two words are spread into a new order

explanation.surface: Fog spread by the French emperor hides a philosopher's ideas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disguising' is a link here. Plotinus (3rd century AD) founded the school that revived and mystified Plato's ideas.
explanation.definitionFit: Plotinus's mystical reworking of Plato's philosophy is the system later called by this name.

clue.text: She was finally trained by Tolstoy

definitions.text: She was finally trained by Tolstoy

parts.words: She was finally trained by Tolstoy
parts.note: Tolstoy's heroine ends her life under a railway carriage, so in the end she was run over by a train rather than educated

explanation.surface: A woman completed her education under the Russian novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trained' seems to mean taught, but the heroine throws herself under a train at the novel's end.
explanation.definitionFit: Tolstoy's tragic heroine dies at a railway station beneath a moving locomotive.

clue.text: The dialect letters found in Cronin's stronghold

indicators.note: the letters of these words are found rearranged in the new title

explanation.surface: Regional speech is discovered in a novelist's fortress.
explanation.walkthrough: A. J. Cronin's 1937 novel The Citadel follows a young Welsh mining-town doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: A citadel is a fortress, and Cronin used the word as the title of his best-known novel.

clue.text: How Eliot's wise men found the towns

definitions.text: How Eliot's wise men found the towns

parts.words: How Eliot's wise men found the towns
parts.note: in Journey of the Magi, T. S. Eliot's travellers find the cities hostile and the towns lacking in welcome

explanation.surface: A question about what the Magi in Eliot's poem made of the settlements on their way.
explanation.walkthrough: The line in Eliot's Journey of the Magi is 'And the cities hostile and the towns unfriendly'.
explanation.definitionFit: Eliot's poem describes the towns as hostile and inhospitable to the three kings.

clue.text: Disraeli heroine associated with the church

definitions.text: Disraeli heroine associated with the church

parts.words: Disraeli heroine associated with the church
parts.note: Disraeli's novel ... Temple names its heroine, whose surname is a place of worship

explanation.surface: A female lead in a Disraeli novel with ecclesiastical links.
explanation.walkthrough: Disraeli's 1837 novel is Henrietta Temple: A Love Story; the 'church' is her surname.
explanation.definitionFit: The heroine of Disraeli's romance is named by this first name, with a house of worship as surname.

clue.text: "Anxiously and — he looked … up the steep ascent of the Aventine" (Bulwer-Lytton, Rienzi)

definitions.text: "Anxiously and — he looked … up the steep ascent of the Aventine" (Bulwer-Lytton, Rienzi)

parts.words: "Anxiously and — he looked … up the steep ascent of the Aventine" (Bulwer-Lytton, Rienzi)
parts.note: the missing word is an adverb paired with anxiously, describing a gaze with tears in the eyes, from Bulwer-Lytton's novel Rienzi

explanation.surface: A quotation from Bulwer-Lytton's novel Rienzi with a word left blank.
explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation: the missing adverb, coupled with 'anxiously', describes a weeping glance up Rome's Aventine hill.
explanation.definitionFit: Weeping while looking, the hero gazes with eyes full of tears, matching the adverb paired with anxiously.

clue.text: It's assuredly Elizabethan

parts.note: an old oath meaning verily or certainly, current in Elizabethan English

explanation.surface: A claim that something is surely from the sixteenth century.
explanation.walkthrough: The word, from French 'par Dieu', is an archaic oath meaning 'certainly', so it is an Elizabethan way of saying 'assuredly'.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic interjection meaning indeed or verily, used by Elizabethan writers.

clue.text: French political historian produces serial, say, with posh following

indicators.note: the letter for posh comes after the grain

parts.note: serial said aloud is cereal, and corn is a cereal
U means upper-class, as in U and non-U

explanation.surface: A French historian writes a serialised work, with an upmarket audience in tow.
explanation.walkthrough: Two steps in 'serial, say': it sounds like 'cereal', of which corn is an example. U for posh is from Nancy Mitford's U and non-U.
explanation.definitionFit: The French historian of politics shares this surname, built from a grain plus an upper-class letter.

clue.text: Provenance of the Grail?

parts.note: legend says Joseph of a certain Judean town brought the cup of the Last Supper to Britain, so his home town is where the Grail came from

explanation.surface: A question about where the Holy Grail came from.
explanation.walkthrough: In Arthurian legend Joseph of Arimathea caught Christ's blood in the Grail and carried it to Glastonbury.
explanation.definitionFit: Joseph, the Grail's legendary bearer, came from this biblical town, so it is the cup's place of origin.

clue.text: Willa Cather booked his house

parts.note: Willa Cather's 1925 novel is titled with an academic's house, so she put his house in a book

explanation.surface: An American novelist made a reservation for a man's home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'booked' looks like reserving, but means put into a book: Cather's novel is The Professor's House.
explanation.definitionFit: Cather's novel concerns Godfrey St Peter, an academic, and the house he cannot leave.

clue.text: Frequent pseudonym of Leon Garfield?

parts.note: the commonest English surname is a stock alias, and Leon Garfield wrote a children's novel of that title about a pickpocket

explanation.surface: Asking which false name the children's author often used.
explanation.walkthrough: Garfield's 1967 novel Smith follows a London pickpocket; the surname is also the stock false name, which makes 'pseudonym' misleading.
explanation.definitionFit: Britain's most common surname is the classic alias for someone hiding their identity, and Garfield's book bears it.

clue.text: God requires zero noise

parts.note: zero looks like the letter O
a din is a loud noise

explanation.surface: A deity demands total silence.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a god wanting no noise; instead zero gives O and noise gives DIN.
explanation.definitionFit: The chief Norse deity, the All-father of Asgard.

clue.text: Very large South American mountain in Greece

parts.note: OS is the clothing abbreviation for outsize
SA stands for South America

explanation.surface: An enormous Andean peak turns out to be in Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: Ossa is the Thessalian mountain the giants piled on Pelion to scale Olympus.
explanation.definitionFit: Mount Ossa in Thessaly is a peak of Greek myth near Olympus and Pelion.

clue.text: Antic of African Queen

definitions.meaning: the founder and ruler of Carthage in North Africa, loved by Aeneas

explanation.surface: The capers of a Hepburn film title.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut a dido' is old slang for playing a prank. The queen of Carthage in Virgil's Aeneid has the same name.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a caper or trick, and also names Carthage's legendary ruler.

clue.text: Cade's alibi broken in Otway piece

indicators.note: an alibi that is broken falls apart, so its letters with those of the name are reassembled

explanation.surface: A rebel's excuse collapses in a Restoration drama.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is a link. Thomas Otway's first tragedy, Alcibiades (1675), is about the Athenian general. Jack Cade led a 1450 English revolt.
explanation.definitionFit: Otway's 1675 tragedy takes its title from the Athenian statesman and general.

clue.text: Old tracks heard of in songs

indicators.note: heard signals that the word for songs is to be sounded, not spelt

parts.note: lays are songs or ballads

explanation.surface: Ancient paths that turn up in ballads.
explanation.walkthrough: Ley lines are supposed prehistoric alignments of ancient sites.
explanation.definitionFit: Ley lines are supposed ancient routes or alignments linking prehistoric sites.

clue.text: Abnormal exaggeration uncovered by V. S. Pritchett?

definitions.text: Abnormal exaggeration uncovered by V. S. Pritchett?

parts.words: Abnormal exaggeration uncovered by V. S. Pritchett?
parts.note: a compulsion to lie or exaggerate, which a writer of Pritchett's biographical essays might expose in his subjects

explanation.surface: A critic exposes wild overstatement.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is 'Abnormal exaggeration'; the rest hints at Pritchett's book The Myth Makers.
explanation.definitionFit: The psychiatric term describes a compulsive tendency to tell tall tales and embroider the truth.
